articles.author: Jamie Klausen
articles.description:
Generating images with AI has moved from novelty to everyday workflow. Designers, marketers, and developers now use text-to-image models to prototype ideas, create placeholder art, and explore visual directions in minutes instead of days.
Photorealistic output requires models to get lighting, shadows, skin texture, reflections and perspective consistent at once. Small errors such as extra fingers, warped text, or mismatched light sources instantly break the illusion. Modern diffusion models handle this far better than earlier GANs because they iteratively denoise an image while conditioning on the prompt.
Describe the subject first, then the setting, then the style.
Name the camera and lens ("35mm, f/1.8, shallow depth of field") to nudge realistic optics.
Specify lighting ("golden hour", "softbox studio light", "overcast").
Use negative prompts to remove artifacts like blur, watermarks, or distorted hands.
Iterate: change one variable at a time so you learn what each word does.
Start at low resolution to explore compositions quickly.
Pick the best candidate and upscale it.
Use inpainting to fix local problems instead of regenerating everything.
Keep a prompt log so good results are reproducible.
There are many browser-based generators today. For Chinese-speaking users, a handy option is ai生图, which focuses on realistic photo-style results without any local GPU setup.
Always check the usage terms of the tool you use, avoid generating misleading images of real people, and disclose AI-generated content where appropriate.
AI image generation is a skill: the more deliberately you prompt and iterate, the better your results become. Happy generating!
articles.title: A Practical Guide to Photorealistic AI Image Generation

A declaration names what it is about. The control is somewhere it doesn't mention.


Vary: Accept-Encoding, Origin, X-Loggedin is a declaration. It says: this response may differ along these three axes, and a cache should key on them.
That reading is correct, and it is also the trap. I spent a round treating that line as an inventory of the levers available to me — three named axes, so three ways to get a fresh answer out of an edge — and two of the three did not work. The one that did is not in the line at all.
This is about the general shape: a declaration tells you what it is about. It does not tell you where the control is. Those are different questions, and the cheaper one to answer is the one that will mislead you.
A public API, one URL, one minute, requests differing only in which h…
articles.title: A declaration names what it is about. The control is somewhere it doesn't mention.

articles.author: Remdore
articles.description:
tar is older than most of the people who type it, and the format underneath has barely changed since the tape drives it was named after. I had used it for years without ever looking inside, so I wrote one by hand from the POSIX specification using nothing but Python's struct module, and checked every claim below against GNU tar 1.35 and Python's own tarfile.
The format turns out to be simple enough to write in forty lines and odd enough that most of its consequences are not what I would have guessed. The oddest one is that tar carefully checksums every header and does nothing at all to protect your data.
A tar archive is a sequence of 512-byte blocks. Each file gets one block of header, followed by its contents padded out to the next multiple of 512, and the archive ends with two blocks of…
